purpose: Bounded official comparator showing physical arrival, formal acceptance, and separately reported first-pilot training completion for a named defense capability while preserving fleet readiness, sustainment, operational-use, and external-response stages.

events.date_precision: official acceptance ceremony date; first three aircraft arrival reported on 2026-05-22
events.denominator: First three Polish F-35 aircraft in one official acceptance record; no fleet-wide or capability-effect denominator
events.method: Structured extraction from the official Polish National Security Bureau event record
events.missingness: Aircraft identifiers, delivery contract line, fleet-wide training coverage, maintenance and sustainment, readiness certification, inventory beyond the first three aircraft, mission use, cost incidence, public response, and geopolitical effect are not retained; the official IOC prerequisites are stated but not shown as achieved
events.exposure: Poland's F-35 modernization program reached physical arrival of the first three aircraft at Łask
events.alternatives_before_action: The official record does not report substitute aircraft, alternative procurement, delay costs, or a counterfactual security path
events.immediate_burden_or_benefit: The first three aircraft were formally accepted into the Polish Armed Forces; the record describes modernization and expected operational-capability significance but does not measure realized readiness
events.choice_or_response: Polish state authorities held an acceptance ceremony and described the aircraft as entering service and strengthening defense potential and the eastern NATO flank
events.person_or_actor_with_control: Polish defense authorities controlled formal acceptance and integration decisions; the public record does not disclose unit-level operational control or readiness certification
events.remedy_or_institutional_response: Formal state acceptance of the aircraft into the Polish Armed Forces was observed
events.remedy_receipt: Not a remedy case; formal acceptance is recorded as an implemented capability milestone, not proof of operational use
events.durability_followup: First-pilot training is separately reported, but fleet-wide maintenance, readiness, mission use, sustainment, and external response remain unobserved in this ledger
events.immediate_outcome: Arrival and formal acceptance of the first three Polish F-35 aircraft are reported in sequence
events.protected_outcome: A named capability crossed from planned procurement into a publicly recorded receiving-state acceptance stage
events.sacrificed_outcome: The record does not establish full operational availability, sustainment, or whether the promised security benefit materialized
events.cost_risk_transfer: The state assumes integration, training, maintenance, and sustainment obligations; public cost incidence and supplier dependence are not measured
events.later_outcome: Official records describe entry into service and first-pilot training, but later fleet operational realization and geopolitical effects remain open
events.meaning_and_attribution: State officials attribute modernization and security significance to the F-35 program; no independent operational or public-legitimacy measure is retained
events.public_or_collective_response: A formal public acceptance ceremony and official statements are observed; allied, adversary, and resident responses are not joined
events.counterexample: Physical arrival and ceremonial acceptance can be publicly documented without proving readiness, durable capability, or geopolitical leverage
events.source_and_uncertainty: Official Polish National Security Bureau and Polish General Command records, https://www.bbn.gov.pl/pl/wydarzenia/10408,Prezydent-RP-na-ceremonii-przyjecia-samolotow-F-35-quotHusarzquot.html and https://www.wojsko-polskie.pl/dgrsz/articles/aktualnosci-w/pierwsi-polscy-piloci-f-35a-lightning-ii-ukonczyli-szkolenie/; the records report arrival, acceptance, and first-pilot training, but do not provide independent fleet-readiness or use telemetry

events.date_precision: official Ministry of National Defence update
events.denominator: Eight Polish F-35 aircraft reported in country; 32 aircraft ordered; no fleet-readiness denominator
events.method: Structured extraction from the official Polish Ministry of National Defence program page
events.missingness: The page reports the eight-aircraft count but does not establish complete pilot and ground-personnel coverage, spare parts and consumables, readiness certification, sortie generation, mission use, sustainment, cost incidence, or external response
events.exposure: The Polish F-35 program reached the stated numeric threshold of eight aircraft in country
events.alternatives_before_action: The official update does not report a substitute capability, alternative procurement, or counterfactual security path
events.immediate_burden_or_benefit: Five additional aircraft joined the first three, increasing the reported in-country fleet to eight; realized operational benefit is not measured
events.choice_or_response: Polish defense authorities continued the staged delivery and public capability-realization process
events.person_or_actor_with_control: Polish defense authorities and program operators control integration, training, sustainment, and readiness decisions; public records do not show certification
events.remedy_or_institutional_response: A further delivery milestone was publicly recorded against the program's stated readiness criterion
events.remedy_receipt: Not a remedy case; the aircraft count is a reported capability milestone, not proof of operational readiness
events.durability_followup: The Ministry states that IOC also requires trained pilots and ground personnel plus spare parts and consumables; later readiness and sustainment remain open
events.immediate_outcome: Official program material reports eight Polish F-35 aircraft after five joined the first three on 28 August 2026
events.protected_outcome: The aircraft-count component of the publicly defined IOC criterion is now observed
events.sacrificed_outcome: The record does not establish full IOC, dependable sortie generation, or changed external behavior
events.cost_risk_transfer: The state assumes additional integration, training, maintenance, and sustainment obligations; supplier dependence and public cost incidence are not measured
events.later_outcome: The route advances from arrival and acceptance to the numeric delivery threshold while personnel, logistics, certification, and strategic effect remain unresolved
events.meaning_and_attribution: The official page presents the delivery as expanding Polish F-35 capability; independent operational and public-legitimacy measures are not retained
events.public_or_collective_response: An official capability update is observed; allied, adversary, and resident responses are not joined
events.counterexample: Meeting an aircraft-count threshold can coexist with unknown training, logistics, certification, readiness, and geopolitical effect
events.source_and_uncertainty: Official Polish Ministry of National Defence page reports that five aircraft joined the first three on 28 August 2026, bringing the total to eight, and separately defines the remaining IOC prerequisites; no independent readiness evidence is retained

arrows.from: Polish F-35 procurement and modernization program
arrows.to: first three aircraft arrive at Łask
arrows.evidence: The official record states that the first three F-35 aircraft landed at the 32nd Tactical Air Base on 22 May 2026
arrows.counterexample: A public arrival statement does not establish contract-line identity, quantity beyond the three aircraft, or operational readiness
arrows.remaining_gap: Identifier-bearing delivery documentation, unit assignment, training, and readiness

arrows.from: first three aircraft arrive at Łask
arrows.to: formal acceptance into the Polish Armed Forces
arrows.evidence: The official record states that the 12 June 2026 ceremony constituted the official acceptance of the aircraft into the Polish Armed Forces
arrows.counterexample: Formal acceptance is not the same as trained, maintained, or mission-ready capability
arrows.remaining_gap: Acceptance instrument, training completion, maintenance, readiness, and operational availability

arrows.to: official claim of strengthened defense potential and eastern-flank security
arrows.evidence: The official record describes the event as strengthening defense potential and the security of the eastern flank
arrows.counterexample: Official strategic meaning is not an observed measure of deterrence, alliance behavior, or security outcome
arrows.remaining_gap: Independent readiness, allied/adversary response, mission use, and geopolitical effect

arrows.to: first Polish F-35 pilots complete training
arrows.evidence: The Polish General Command reports that the first Polish F-35A pilots completed training after theoretical, simulator, and practical instruction; this is a personnel/training milestone rather than fleet readiness
arrows.counterexample: Training completion for first pilots does not establish all-pilot coverage, maintenance capacity, sortie generation, or mission readiness
arrows.remaining_gap: Training coverage, aircraft-pilot assignment, maintenance, availability, and readiness certification

arrows.evidence: The Polish Ministry of National Defence states that initial operational capability requires at least eight aircraft in Poland, the necessary trained pilots and ground personnel, and required spare parts and consumables
arrows.counterexample: A stated readiness threshold is a governance criterion, not evidence that the threshold has been met
arrows.remaining_gap: Eight-aircraft threshold, full pilot and ground-personnel coverage, spare parts, consumables, and readiness certification

arrows.to: eight Polish F-35 aircraft reported in country
arrows.evidence: The official Ministry of National Defence page reports that five aircraft joined the first three on 28 August 2026, increasing the Polish F-35 count to eight
arrows.counterexample: An in-country aircraft count does not establish serviceability, training coverage, or mission availability
arrows.remaining_gap: Aircraft identifiers, serviceability, assigned crews, maintenance, and sortie generation

arrows.evidence: The official Ministry page defines IOC as requiring eight aircraft plus trained pilots and ground personnel and necessary spares and consumables; only the eight-aircraft component is newly observed
arrows.counterexample: The numeric threshold can be met while the personnel, logistics, certification, readiness, and mission-use conditions remain unknown
arrows.remaining_gap: Trained ground-personnel coverage, spares, consumables, readiness certification, operational availability, and mission use

arrows.from: accepted aircraft, first-pilot training, and IOC prerequisites
arrows.to: durable operational capability and geopolitical leverage
arrows.evidence: Official records report arrival, acceptance, first-pilot training, and the IOC definition, but no independent fleet-readiness, sustainment, mission-use, or external-response measure
arrows.counterexample: Partial human preparation and a stated threshold can coexist with unknown fleet availability, sustainment, operational use, and changed external behavior
arrows.remaining_gap: Fleet readiness, maintenance, mission use, sustainment, cost, allied/adversary response, and strategic effect

boundary: This ledger is a comparator for the capability-realization chain. It establishes public arrival and formal acceptance for the first three aircraft, not full fleet realization, readiness, operational use, or geopolitical leverage.
storage_boundary: No classified, telemetry, personnel, or restricted procurement file is retained; only bounded official public-record fields and open downstream stages are represented.
